claim: REVIEW-LEVEL SYNTHESIS, not primary causal evidence: this 2025 paper surveys variable impedance/admittance control for human-robot interaction with emphasis on nonlinear, fuzzy, fractional-order, hybrid, and learning-based approaches. It argues that the field still predominantly uses linear mass-damping-stiffness interaction models, with learning often tuning coefficients rather than replacing the linear structure, while nonlinear or fractional/fuzzy models may better express hysteresis, frequency dependence, uncertainty, and context-dependent human behavior at the price of computation, tuning burden, and reduced interpretability. Although titled a systematic review, the supplied full text does not report a reproducible database search, query, screening flow, eligibility criteria, date boundary, duplicate handling, or study-quality/risk-of-bias assessment; its favorable performance and safety conclusions are therefore narrative author synthesis of heterogeneous cited studies, not systematic comparative or causal evidence.
claim_locator: Section 3 and Table 1, industrial cobot applications
Section 5.1-5.3, equations (4)-(27), Tables 2 and related figures
epistemic_status: self-described systematic review, but evidentially narrative: full text verified and useful for broad landscape mapping, yet no reproducible review protocol or study-level quality assessment is present; claims of improvement are mainly paraphrased from heterogeneous source papers without common metrics or meta-analysis
problem_and_setting: The paper addresses selection of interaction controllers for Industry 4.0/5.0 HRI/HRC, where robots must adapt to human motion, contact conditions, uncertainty, and nonlinear physiology. It focuses on whether linear variable impedance/admittance models are sufficient and how fuzzy logic, fractional-order dynamics, hybrid controllers, and learning methods can improve adaptability, robustness, force tracking, and safety.
method_or_mechanism: The article narratively assembles prior HRI/HRC, cobot-application, VIC/VAC, nonlinear-model, fuzzy-control, fractional-order, and learning literature. Its technical taxonomy contrasts the standard linear mass-damping-stiffness model with nonlinear gain scheduling and contextual/physiological models; fuzzy systems infer or adapt gains from linguistic rules or uncertainty; fractional-order derivatives add frequency- and memory-dependent dynamics; hybrid fuzzy-fractional/sliding-mode/neural controllers combine uncertainty approximation and robust tracking; learning methods estimate intentions, trajectories, dynamics, or impedance policies. The review does not expose a formal study-identification or appraisal mechanism.
content_summary: The first sections review HRI/HRC definitions, collaboration levels, human factors, standards, sensors, and industrial applications. The control sections explain impedance/admittance and survey energy reservoirs, stability-constrained VIC, adaptive force tracking, sensorless variants, and fuzzy adaptation. A dedicated comparison argues that linear models are simple and interpretable but cannot fully capture nonlinear, hysteretic human joints or rapid contact changes; nonlinear models may improve fidelity but require more computation, data, and tuning. The fractional-order sections cover fuzzy FOPID, fractional sliding-mode, type-II fuzzy, and variable fractional admittance examples, many of which are simulations or low-DOF platforms rather than direct pHRI trials. The final section surveys fuzzy VIC/VAC and learning via neural networks, demonstrations, reinforcement learning, model-predictive control, and repetitive learning. The conclusion reports broad benefits but also reiterates that linear models dominate and that accuracy-complexity trade-offs remain.
synthesis_role: Provides a recent, unusually broad catalog of fuzzy and fractional-order control ideas adjacent to variable impedance HRI. Its best use is hypothesis generation and terminology mapping. It should not be used alone to infer that nonlinear/fuzzy/fractional controllers outperform classical VIC or improve human safety across applications.
development_link: Extends earlier impedance reviews by emphasizing the linear-to-nonlinear modeling transition and by grouping fractional calculus, type-I/type-II fuzzy logic, sliding mode, neural estimation, reinforcement learning, and MPC as routes to adaptive interaction. It highlights a continuing gap between increasingly complex gain-tuning machinery and the largely linear impedance structures being tuned.

evidence.finding: The authors conclude that linear interaction models with unknown coefficients remain dominant and that learning methods commonly optimize those coefficients rather than replace the underlying linear structure.
HRI/HRC levels, human factors, standards, sensors, and cobot applications are cataloged across manufacturing, health care, agriculture, aerospace, logistics, construction, and hazardous work.

Reviewed VIC/VAC approaches adjust stiffness, damping, or inertia through energy reservoirs, stability-constrained profiles, environment estimation, fuzzy adaptation, sensorless inference, or learning; the article notes that energy injection can threaten passivity.

Linear models are judged simple and interpretable but limited for nonlinear/hysteretic human behavior and fast contact variation; nonlinear models offer richer adaptation while increasing computation, tuning, data demand, and interpretability problems.

Fuzzy fractional-order, fractional sliding-mode, type-II fuzzy, and variable fractional admittance controllers are reported across simulations, low-DOF manipulators, exoskeletons, haptics, polishing, teleoperation, and other systems, with no common benchmark or pooled effect.

Fuzzy and learning-based controllers estimate human intent, environment properties, trajectories, or impedance parameters using neural networks, demonstrations, RL, MPC, and iterative learning; evidence types range from simulation to small robot demonstrations.

The paper claims improved adaptability, responsiveness, flexibility, safety, and error reduction from fractional, fuzzy, and learning methods, while acknowledging that nonlinear accuracy gains directly increase system complexity.

evidence.status: methodological limitation observed in supplied text
evidence.finding: No database list, search string, search dates, PRISMA-style flow, inclusion/exclusion criteria, duplicate procedure, extraction protocol, study-quality appraisal, or quantitative synthesis is reported.

boundary_conditions: Despite the title, the supplied article does not document reproducible systematic-review methods; completeness and selection bias cannot be assessed.
The 247 references span reviews, theory, simulations, low-DOF robots, non-HRI control examples, industrial applications, and pHRI experiments, so they do not form a uniform causal evidence base.
No study-level risk-of-bias or quality grading, sample-size synthesis, standardized outcome definition, or meta-analysis is provided.
Reported percentage improvements and performance claims are carried over from individual source papers with different baselines and conditions.

Some fuzzy/fractional examples concern generic nonlinear systems, mobile robots, wind turbines, self-balancing robots, or tracking controllers rather than direct interaction-port impedance in human-robot tasks.
Safety is discussed largely as an intended or reported benefit; the review does not aggregate collision injury, force-limit, clinical, or human-subject safety outcomes.
The publication includes references from 2025 but does not state a search cutoff, making temporal coverage nonreproducible.
More complex nonlinear controllers may require computation, sensing, training data, and tuning unavailable on the platforms represented by simpler linear models.
assumptions: The cited studies' reported simulations and experiments were accurately characterized by the review authors.
Fractional-order and fuzzy formulations capture task-relevant memory, frequency dependence, nonlinearity, or uncertainty rather than merely adding tunable degrees of freedom.
Performance metrics from heterogeneous applications are directionally comparable enough to support broad qualitative conclusions.
The underlying impedance/admittance port model remains meaningful when combined with learning and nonlinear gain adaptation.
Stability proofs based on Lyapunov, passivity, or boundedness in individual studies apply to the implementation actually tested.
The selected literature is representative despite the absent search and screening documentation.

reported: Linear impedance models cannot fully represent nonlinear, hysteretic human musculoskeletal behavior or rapidly changing interaction conditions.
VIC can introduce energy and jeopardize passivity/stability; VAC can have difficulty distinguishing divergent forces from error-related forces.
Nonlinear accuracy and robustness gains come with greater model complexity, computation, tuning, and interpretability burden.
Many fractional-order robotic-control studies focus on one- to three-joint systems, leaving industrial manipulators with more than five joints underexplored.
Several fuzzy/fractional methods show only simulation evidence, and real-world implementation requires further study.
Learning methods commonly optimize parameters within a linear impedance structure rather than learn a genuinely nonlinear interaction law.
inferred: Labeling the article systematic overstates methodological rigor because core systematic-review procedures are absent from the supplied text.
Narrative aggregation of favorable source results is vulnerable to publication, citation, and confirmation bias.
Mixing generic control and non-HRI examples with pHRI/VIC studies can inflate the apparent maturity of fuzzy fractional impedance control for human interaction.
Greater controller flexibility can increase identifiability problems, overfitting, implementation mismatch, and unverified behavior outside the training or tuning region.
Broad safety claims are not supported by a dedicated synthesis of human-subject adverse events, collision metrics, or standards compliance.
Without shared benchmarks, it is not possible to determine whether gains arise from fractional order, fuzzy inference, optimization effort, controller order, or different experimental conditions.
